client: I just don't know how to function normally after losing my grandma. Some days I'm fine, then suddenly I'll see something that reminds me of her and I can't focus on anything for hours. My boss has noticed I'm making mistakes at work, but the more I try to push through it, the worse it gets.
therapist: It sounds like you're experiencing waves of grief that come unexpectedly, and the pressure to perform at work while dealing with this loss is making it even harder. The way your voice quickens when talking about these moments tells me how overwhelming these memories feel when they surface. Would it help to explore some ways to create space for your grief while also managing work responsibilities?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I guess creating space for grief sounds nice in theory, but I don’t see how it’s possible when work demands so much of me. Every time I try to pause and let myself feel, I just end up feeling guilty for not being productive. It’s like I’m stuck between needing to grieve and needing to keep up with everything else.
therapist: I hear both frustration and urgency in your voice as you describe this impossible tension between grieving and working - that tightness when you feel pulled in two directions at once. Let's examine that guilt you mentioned - what evidence do you have that taking time to process your loss actually makes you less productive in the long run?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess I don't have concrete evidence, but it just feels like if I stop to grieve, I'll fall behind at work permanently. My boss keeps saying "take all the time you need," but I hear the unspoken deadline pressure in every team meeting. The guilt comes from knowing others are picking up my slack while I'm... stuck.
therapist: The way your voice lifts when talking about deadlines tells me how much this pressure weighs on you, even when others offer support on the surface. Let's challenge that fear of "falling behind permanently" - have you considered that allowing yourself to process now might actually help you return to your full capacity sooner?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying, but it’s hard to believe that taking time to process will actually help me catch up. When I slow down, I just feel more guilty and anxious, like I’m wasting time I don’t have. Deadlines keep piling up, and it feels like if I stop, I’ll never get back on track.
therapist: I notice your voice gets quieter when talking about slowing down, like part of you is already bracing for that wave of guilt. That anxious feeling about wasted time might actually be your grief trying to tell you something important - what if honoring these moments could eventually help you work with more focus when you do return to tasks?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client:
I never thought about it that way... but when you say that, I can feel this tightness in my chest. It's like part of me knows I need breaks, but another part screams that I'm being lazy. Even now, I'm glancing at the clock thinking about all the emails I should be answering instead of sitting here. 

The grief idea makes sense, but it's hard to sit with. Wouldn't I just feel worse if I actually let myself slow down?
therapist: I hear how conflicted you feel - that tightness in your chest matching the way your voice speeds up when torn between self-care and responsibilities. Let's explore what "lazy" really means here - could it be that honoring your grief is actually the most courageous and productive thing you could do for your long-term wellbeing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I don't know if I'd call it courageous. It just feels selfish. Like I should be able to push through my grief and keep up with everything like normal people do. When I take time for myself, I just end up feeling guilty about all the things I'm not getting done.
therapist: I hear how conflicted and anxious you feel about taking time for yourself - your voice sounds strained when you talk about pushing through, like you're carrying a heavy weight. Let's examine that idea of "normal people" - where did you learn that grieving requires pushing through rather than processing these feelings?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I learned it from my parents - they always just kept going no matter what happened. When my grandma died, my dad was back at work the next day. But now that you mention it, I feel like maybe that's why I'm so exhausted all the time. It's just... what if stopping to process makes everything worse? What if I can't handle what comes up?
therapist: Your voice speeds up as you share this family pattern, and I hear both exhaustion and fear in how you describe it - like you're torn between two painful options: continuing this exhausting cycle or risking facing emotions you've been taught to avoid. The fact that you're questioning this pattern now shows real courage - what if honoring your grief could actually be the path to feeling *less* exhausted, even if the process feels hard at first?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, but the thought of actually facing that grief feels terrifying. What if I get overwhelmed and can't handle it? I've always been told to stay strong and keep going, so opening up that box feels like I'm betraying everything I was taught. Plus, I don't even know where to start—it’s all so tangled up.
therapist: I hear the fear in your quickened, higher voice as you talk about opening up this pain - it makes complete sense that facing grief feels terrifying when you've only known how to push through it. That "betrayal" feeling is important to notice - could we slow down and explore what "staying strong" has really cost you over the years?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: Staying strong has cost me so much—I feel like I’ve lost touch with who I really am. I’ve spent years pushing through the pain, but now it feels like I’m carrying this heavy weight that I don’t even know how to put down. It’s scary to think about stopping and actually feeling all of it—what if I fall apart and can’t put myself back together?
therapist: Your voice trembles with both exhaustion and fear as you describe this weight you've carried for so long - I can hear how terrifying it feels to imagine setting it down. That fear of falling apart makes perfect sense when you've never allowed yourself to truly feel these emotions before. What if we explored this together slowly, at a pace that feels safe enough to begin unpacking what "falling apart" really means to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I feel so exposed when you point out how scared I am to let go. Part of me wants to push back and say I'm fine, but another part knows you're right. It's just... what if I start crying and can't stop? What if I completely lose control and can't pull myself back together? The thought of fully feeling these emotions terrifies me because I don't know what's on the other side of that.
therapist: I hear how raw and vulnerable this feels for you - your voice rises sharply when talking about losing control, like you're standing at the edge of something overwhelming. That fear of the unknown on "the other side" is completely understandable when grief has been locked away for so long. Could we explore what control has given you all these years, and what it might look like to loosen your grip just a little at a time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
